summary: Provides procedures for registering extensible LDAP elements, and tells IANA the conditions under which new values can be assigned. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: The rules for adding a new item to the official LDAP list, so no two people claim the same name.

subtitle: How to register new LDAP extensions and protocol elements.

tldr.problem: LDAP is an extensible protocol that supports new operations, extensions to existing operations, and extensible schema elements. Without a standardized registration process, extensions could conflict or go undocumented.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4520 establishes IANA registries and registration procedures for LDAP elements such as message types, controls, result codes, authentication methods, object identifier descriptors, and schema options. Different elements follow different registration policies (Standards Action, Expert Review, or First Come First Served).
tldr.outcome: The document provides a stable, well-documented way to extend LDAP. It replaces RFC 3383 and serves as the current Best Current Practice for LDAP extensibility.

facts.label: Registerable element types
facts.value: 13 categories: OIDs, protocol mechanisms, syntaxes, descriptors, options, message types, auth methods

facts.label: Registration policies
facts.value: Standards Action, Expert Review, First Come First Served

today: RFC 4520 is an Internet Best Current Practice and remains the authoritative document for LDAP registration procedures. It has not been obsoleted, so it is still the definition of how to extend LDAP in a registered, interoperable way.

sections.title: What LDAP Needs to Register
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is designed to be extended. It allows new operations, extensions to existing operations, and changes to its schema. RFC 4520 defines how to register these extensible elements so they do not conflict.

The elements that need registration include LDAP message types, extended operations and controls, result codes, authentication methods, attribute description options, Object Identifier descriptors, LDAP syntaxes, and other protocol mechanisms. These registries are maintained by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).
sections.eli5: When you add a new piece to LDAP, it needs an official number or name so nobody else uses the same one. IANA keeps the official list.

sections.title: Terms and Registration Policies
sections.content:
The RFC defines registration policies based on the type of element being registered. Standards Action requires approval by the IETF standards process and is used for the most important extensions. Expert Review allows faster registration under guidance from a designated expert but still requires specification. First Come First Served is the fastest: a requester submits a form directly to IANA with minimal review.

The RFC also distinguishes between the registration owner (the party authorized to change a registration) and the role of IANA as the registry maintainer.
sections.eli5: There are different levels of checking depending on how risky the change is. Important changes go through strict review, while simple additions can be registered faster.

sections.title: What Gets Registered and How
sections.content:
The RFC specifies registration procedures for 13 categories of LDAP elements.

Object Identifiers (OIDs) identify most LDAP elements. IETF-developed elements typically use the 1.3.6.1.1.x arc and are registered by Expert Review with Specification Required. Private enterprises use 1.3.6.1.4.1.x and 1.3.6.1.3.x for experimental OIDs. Protocol Mechanisms (controls, extensions, features) are registered First Come First Served. LDAP Syntaxes require First Come First Served with Specification Required.

Object Identifier Descriptors are short names for OIDs. Descriptors starting with x- are reserved for private use; those starting with e- are for experiments. All others require Expert Review. AttributeDescription Options allow additional semantics on attributes and follow similar rules: x- is private use, e- requires First Come First Served, and others require Standards Action or Expert Review.

LDAP Message Types, Authentication Methods, Result Codes, Search Scope values, Filter Choices, and ModifyRequest Operation Types all follow tiered policies: the lowest numeric ranges (0-1023) require Standards Action, mid-ranges (1024-4095) require Expert Review, and higher ranges (4096-16383) use First Come First Served. Private use and experimental ranges are reserved.

authzId Prefixes identify authorization identity forms and follow the same x- and e- conventions as descriptors and options.

Directory Systems Names, a legacy LDAPv2 registry, are no longer accepted for new registrations.
sections.eli5: Different LDAP features have different rules for getting a registered number. The most critical things need approval from the IETF, medium-importance ones need an expert to check them, and simple additions can be registered right away.

sections.title: How to Register a New Element
sections.content:
A requester begins by completing a registration template (included in the RFC appendix) describing the extension. The template content varies by element type but always asks for the requester's contact information, a specification (an RFC, Internet Draft, or URI), and the author/change controller.

For Standards Action registrations, the form goes to the IESG with a request for Standards Action. The IESG reviews and, if approved, forwards it to IANA and is regarded as the registration owner.

For Expert Review registrations, the form is posted to the LDAP mailing list for a two-week public review period. Anyone may object, and the Expert makes the final decision based on public comments, then notifies the requester. The requester becomes the registration owner.

For First Come First Served registrations, the requester submits the form directly to IANA, who processes it with no further review. The requester is the registration owner.

Before an Internet Draft becomes an RFC, the document editor should update it to use registered values where possible.
sections.eli5: You fill out a form describing your new feature. Depending on how risky it is, the form either gets looked at by IETF experts, a single expert, or just goes straight to IANA.

sections.title: Maintaining Registrations
sections.content:
IANA publishes the list of registered values on its web site for public access. The registration owner may update a registration subject to the same constraints as a new registration. If the owner is unable or unwilling to update, the IESG may take ownership of the registration in order to make necessary updates.

If others have significant objections to a registration and the owner refuses to change it, comments may be attached to the registration after Expert Review. For registrations owned by the IESG, objections are addressed by requesting Expert Review.
sections.eli5: Once something is registered, the person who registered it can update it. If they won't keep it up to date, the IETF can take it over. Other people can add comments if they disagree with what is registered.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4520 notes that the security considerations in BCP 26 (RFC 2434, Guidelines for IANA Considerations in RFCs) generally apply. Different LDAP element categories may have additional security considerations, some of which are discussed in Section 3 of this RFC.

Security considerations for LDAP overall are covered in the LDAP technical specification documents, particularly RFC 4510 and its related RFCs.
sections.eli5: When you add something to LDAP, you need to think about whether it creates security problems. The RFC reminds people to check the LDAP security documentation.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 3383
sections.content:
RFC 4520 obsoletes RFC 3383. Key changes include updated practices for Object Identifier Descriptors (now requiring registration for all descriptors in RFCs and recommending registration for others); inclusion of supportedFeatures attribute values in Protocol Mechanisms; and addition of new registries for LDAP Syntaxes, Search Scope, Filter Choice, ModifyRequest Operation Type, and authzId Prefixes.

References were updated to the latest LDAP technical specification RFCs, and references to ISO 10646 were replaced with the Unicode standard. An earlier appendix listing initial registry values was removed, and numerous editorial improvements were made.
sections.eli5: The RFC fixes and expands what RFC 3383 did. It adds several new kinds of things that can be registered and makes the procedures clearer.
